title: Why Cannabis Rescheduling Changes Everything for Glass House Brands
summary: Jonathan DeCourcey argues that medical rescheduling can transform Glass House by opening higher-priced markets, lowering taxes and enabling a US listing. Eisman explicitly adopts the speculative margin thesis in his recap. The NYSE listing and first European hemp sale occurred, while the guest's pre-fall broad-rescheduling deadline failed. Export permits and state rules remain material, European cultivation already exists, and the proposed Medicare market is overstated. Eisman also converts a production-cost target into a current figure and confuses illustrative gross margin with operating margin. The larger earnings opportunity remains conditional.
assessment: The successful listing and hemp export are distinct from unproven interstate medical-cannabis economics. Guest errors are recorded separately; Eisman is responsible only for his explicit claims and closing adoption. The investment thesis remains unresolved, while its legal, cost and margin premises contain identifiable errors.
speaker_map_notes: SPEAKER_01 is Steve Eisman and SPEAKER_00 is Jonathan DeCourcey, identified as Glass House head of investor relations. Very short interjections are occasionally embedded within the other speaker's segment; attribution follows the surrounding question and response.
framework_points: Compare a restricted local market with potential expanded-market economics.
Separate current operations, installed capacity, targets and realized production.
Treat legal reform, licensing and distribution implementation as distinct milestones.
Use price-volume-cost scenarios while retaining incremental expenses.
Separate a successful exchange listing from investment returns and operating success.
Disclose ownership and distinguish speculative opportunity from modeled valuation.
tools_and_charts: Greenhouse footprint and annual biomass capacity
Cost per pound and wholesale prices
California versus US medical and European market pricing
Reverse stock split and exchange-listing conditions

DeCorsi is normalized to Jonathan DeCourcey from the identified company role.
The guest repeatedly says April 18; the inspected medical rule was issued April 23 and published April 28.
The 1920-second can/cannot institutional-ownership interjection is ambiguous and is not silently corrected.
The guest initially says target selling price then explicitly corrects to target production cost.
Eisman's closing operating-margin language differs from the guest's gross-margin calculation.
Publication follows June retail deconsolidation; original interview figures describe the earlier business perimeter.
The first completed European transaction was hemp; it is not evidence of unrestricted marijuana exports.

claims.deductive_proof: Gross margin = (price-cost)/price. At cost $100, margins are 50% at price $200, 87.5% at $800 and 90% at $1,000. This is unit gross margin, not consolidated operating margin.
